chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Sayyari who said:

Muhammad ibn al-Faraj wrote to al-Askari (peace be upon him) asking him about what has been narrated regarding the calculation for fasting from your forefathers — specifically counting five days between the first of the past year and the second year that is coming.

So he (the Imam) wrote back: 'Correct. But count five (days) for every four years, and in the fifth year count six, between the former and the new (year). As for the rest, it is (always) five and five.'
Al-Sayyari said: 'This is due to the matter of the leap year.' He said: 'Our companions have calculated it and found it to be correct.'

He said: 'And Muhammad ibn al-Faraj wrote to him in the year 238 (AH): This calculation is not feasible for every person to act upon. Rather, this is only for the one who understands the yearly cycles and knows when the leap year falls, and then the crescent of the month of Ramadan is confirmed for him on the first night. So when the crescent is confirmed for its night and he knows the years, it will be correct for him, if God wills.'

key_terms.الحساب: Calendrical reckoning/calculation — here referring to a method for determining the start of lunar months using solar intercalation
key_terms.السنة الكبيسة: The leap year — a year with an intercalary day to keep the solar calendar synchronized
key_terms.الكبيسة: The leap year (al-kabisa) — the Julian calendar's four-year cycle adding an extra day, here used to reconcile solar and lunar calendars for fasting determination
key_terms.الهلال: The new crescent moon (hilal) — the sighting of which marks the beginning of Ramadan in Islamic lunar calendar practice

ai.seo_question: How did Imam al-Askari determine the start of Ramadan using a leap year calculation?
ai.summary: In this legal ruling from Imam Hasan al-Askari (AS), communicated through written correspondence with Muhammad ibn al-Faraj around 238 AH, the Imam confirms a calendar-based method for determining the start of Ramadan fasting. The method involves counting five intercalary days between consecutive years in a four-year cycle, with six days counted in the fifth year — a reference to the Julian leap year cycle. Al-Sayyari, the narrator, identifies this as relating to the leap year (al-kabisa), and notes that Shia scholars verified the method mathematically. A second letter from Muhammad ibn al-Faraj notes that this calculation requires knowledge of the solar calendar cycle and the ability to confirm the new crescent moon.
